--- title: 'Week 4: pandas for economic data' --- [Open in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/WSU-EconS431/site/blob/main/weeks/week04.ipynb) · [View on GitHub](https://github.com/WSU-EconS431/site/blob/main/weeks/week04.ipynb) So far the data in this course has been numbers we typed or drew at random. Real economic data arrives as tables: rows of countries, firms, or quarters, and columns of variables with units and gaps. **pandas** is the Python tool for tables. It selects rows by condition (like Week 3's Boolean masks), computes new columns, summarizes by group, and combines tables. **After this week you can:** - load a CSV file into a DataFrame and check its shape, types, units, and gaps before using it - select columns and rows, including by condition, and sort - create new columns and handle missing values without distorting an average - summarize by group with `groupby` and combine two tables with `merge`, checking row counts - reshape between long and wide tables and work with dates All the data this week are real, from the course's `data` folder. [data/README.md](https://github.com/WSU-EconS431/site/blob/main/data/README.md) gives each source, the download date, and any changes. ::: {#8ede339a .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.134780Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.134337Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.707091Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.705402Z"}}' execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from pathlib import Path # The course data live in the site repo's data folder. In Colab, read them from GitHub instead. DATA = "../data" if Path("../data").exists() else "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WSU-EconS431/site/main/data" ``` ::: ## 1. Series and DataFrames A **DataFrame** is a table: named columns, one value per row in each. Each column is a **Series**, which is like a Week 3 array that also carries row labels (the **index**). We start with a made-up table of a market's prices and quantities by year. ::: {#7f4388cf .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.709075Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.708766Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.721282Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.720068Z"}}' execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} market = pd.DataFrame({ "year": [2019, 2020, 2021, 2022], "price": [28.0, 24.5, 31.0, 36.5], "quantity": [52, 61, 47, 40], }) market ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
year price quantity
0 2019 28.0 52
1 2020 24.5 61
2 2021 31.0 47
3 2022 36.5 40
``` ::: ::: Arithmetic on columns works on every row at once, as with arrays, and assigning to a new name creates a column: ::: {#06ea35dc .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.723150Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.722897Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.733761Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.731463Z"}}' execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} market["revenue"] = market["price"] * market["quantity"] print(market.shape, list(market.columns)) print("mean price:", market["price"].mean(), " highest revenue:", market["revenue"].max()) market ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (4, 4) ['year', 'price', 'quantity', 'revenue'] mean price: 30.0 highest revenue: 1494.5 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
year price quantity revenue
0 2019 28.0 52 1456.0
1 2020 24.5 61 1494.5
2 2021 31.0 47 1457.0
3 2022 36.5 40 1460.0
``` ::: ::: Setting a column as the **index** lets you look rows up by label. `.loc[row label, column name]` is the label-based lookup: ::: {#f16b18f5 .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.735770Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.735551Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.740561Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.739538Z"}}' execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} by_year = market.set_index("year") by_year.loc[2021, "price"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` np.float64(31.0) ``` ::: ::: ## 2. Loading a real dataset The **Maddison Project Database** (2020 release) estimates GDP per capita and population for 169 countries over a very long span. `gdppc` is GDP per capita in 2011 international dollars (adjusted so a dollar buys the same amount in every country), and `pop` is population in **thousands**. Check the units before computing anything. ::: {#25f02f40 .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.742383Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.742186Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.762529Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.761709Z"}}' execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} mpd = pd.read_csv(f"{DATA}/mpd2020_full.csv") mpd.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
countrycode country year gdppc pop
0 AFG Afghanistan 1820 NaN 3280.0
1 AFG Afghanistan 1870 NaN 4207.0
2 AFG Afghanistan 1913 NaN 5730.0
3 AFG Afghanistan 1950 1156.0 8150.0
4 AFG Afghanistan 1951 1170.0 8284.0
``` ::: ::: ::: {#1998ee8e .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.764626Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.764442Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.775601Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.774248Z"}}' execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(mpd.shape) mpd.info() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (21682, 5) RangeIndex: 21682 entries, 0 to 21681 Data columns (total 5 columns): # Column Non-Null Count Dtype --- ------ -------------- ----- 0 countrycode 21682 non-null str 1 country 21682 non-null str 2 year 21682 non-null int64 3 gdppc 19706 non-null float64 4 pop 17199 non-null float64 dtypes: float64(2), int64(1), str(2) memory usage: 847.1 KB ``` ::: ::: ::: {#7fd06c98 .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.777334Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.777129Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.792593Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.791135Z"}}' execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} mpd.describe() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}
year gdppc pop

``` ::: ::: Look at the `min` of `gdppc`: it is 0.0, but no country has zero GDP per capita. Find those rows: ::: {#5b4b5b15 .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.794376Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.794178Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.801589Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.800616Z"}}' execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} mpd[mpd['gdppc'] <= 0] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}
countrycode country year gdppc pop
293 ARE United Arab Emirates 1991 0.0 1934.841255
294 ARE United Arab Emirates 1992 0.0 2050.441137
``` ::: ::: Two rows, the United Arab Emirates in 1991 and 1992, have a GDP per capita of zero and a population of about two million. That is almost certainly a placeholder for "no estimate", not a real zero, and it would break any calculation with logs (`np.log(0)` is $-\infty$). We treat these as missing in our working copy. The snapshot file stays exactly as downloaded, and the change is recorded here, in the notebook. ::: {#1b2e7202 .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.803194Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.802984Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.807383Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.806495Z"}}' execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} mpd.loc[mpd["gdppc"] <= 0, "gdppc"] = np.nan print("smallest gdppc now:", mpd["gdppc"].min()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` smallest gdppc now: 295.0 ``` ::: ::: Three questions to ask of any new table, before any analysis: 1. **What is a row?** Here, one country in one year. The same country appears many times. 2. **What are the units?** Dollars per person, thousands of people. 3. **What is covered?** The `year` column starts at 1, and some countries start much later than others. ::: {#04926acb .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.808737Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.808562Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.817887Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.816815Z"}}' execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} print("countries:", mpd["country"].nunique()) print("years:", mpd["year"].min(), "to", mpd["year"].max()) mpd[mpd["country"].str.startswith("Former")]["country"].unique() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` countries: 169 years: 1 to 2018 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` ['Former USSR', 'Former Yugoslavia'] Length: 2, dtype: str ``` ::: ::: Look at that last result: some rows describe regions that no longer exist as countries (the "Former" rows), and the successor countries, such as the Russian Federation, appear as rows of their own. Adding up rows across countries would count that territory twice. Reading the data's documentation is part of the analysis. ## 3. Selecting columns and rows One column in brackets gives a Series; a **list** of column names gives a DataFrame: ::: {#07fb3714 .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.820305Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.820011Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.826537Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.825934Z"}}' execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(mpd["gdppc"].head(3)) mpd[["country", "year", "gdppc"]].head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0 NaN 1 NaN 2 NaN Name: gdppc, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}
country year gdppc
0 Afghanistan 1820 NaN
1 Afghanistan 1870 NaN
2 Afghanistan 1913 NaN
``` ::: ::: A comparison gives a Boolean mask, exactly as in Week 3, and putting the mask inside the brackets keeps the rows where it is `True`. Combine conditions with `&` (and), `|` (or), and `~` (not), with **parentheses around each condition**: ::: {#65e9f330 .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.828185Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.827992Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.844245Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.842924Z"}}' execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} usa = mpd[mpd["countrycode"] == "USA"] japan_recent = mpd[(mpd["country"] == "Japan") & (mpd["year"] >= 2000)] print(usa.shape, japan_recent.shape) japan_recent.head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (227, 5) (19, 5) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}
countrycode country year gdppc pop
10626 JPN Japan 2000 33210.8078 126933.1312
10627 JPN Japan 2001 33246.3921 127234.3736
10628 JPN Japan 2002 33195.4005 127502.5894
``` ::: ::: Python's `and` doesn't work here, for the same reason `if` didn't work on arrays in Week 3: a comparison on a column gives many `True`/`False` values, not one. ::: {#16ff760e .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.846636Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.846414Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.919970Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.918184Z"}}' tags='["raises-exception"]' execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} mpd[(mpd["country"] == "Japan") and (mpd["year"] >= 2000)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

----> 1 mpd[(mpd["country"] == "Japan") and (mpd["year"] >= 2000)]

File ~\EconS431\instructor\.venv\Lib\site-packages\pandas\core\generic.py:1501, in NDFrame.__bool__(self)

   1504         )

ValueError: The truth value of a Series is ambiguous. Use a.empty, a.bool(), a.item(), a.any() or a.all().
``` ::: ::: ::: `.query` writes the same filter as a string, and `.loc[rows, columns]` picks rows and columns together. `.sort_values` orders the rows; `.isin` tests membership in a list. ::: {#478221a9 .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.921722Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.921539Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.936028Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.935268Z"}}' execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(mpd.query("year == 2018 and gdppc > 60000")[["country", "gdppc"]]) y2018 = mpd[mpd["year"] == 2018] rich = y2018.sort_values("gdppc", ascending=False) print(rich[["country", "gdppc"]].head(5)) y2018.nsmallest(5, "gdppc")[["country", "gdppc"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` country gdppc 320 United Arab Emirates 76397.8181 2699 Switzerland 61372.7301 9228 Ireland 64684.3020 11106 Kuwait 65520.7367 14560 Norway 84580.1362 17166 Qatar 153764.1643 17797 Singapore 68402.3451 country gdppc 17166 Qatar 153764.1643 14560 Norway 84580.1362 320 United Arab Emirates 76397.8181 17797 Singapore 68402.3451 11106 Kuwait 65520.7367 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ```{=html}
country gdppc
2336 Central African Republic 623.4889
1084 Burundi 651.3589
11319 Liberia 818.4211

``` ::: ::: ::: {#b934b875 .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.937775Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.937588Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.944983Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.943733Z"}}' execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} big3 = mpd[mpd["country"].isin(["China", "India", "Japan"])] big3["country"].value_counts() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ``` country China 243 Japan 212 India 208 Name: count, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: ## 4. New columns, units, and a gotcha Total GDP is GDP per capita times population. Since `pop` is in thousands, $\text{gdppc} \times \text{pop}$ is in thousands of dollars, and dividing by $10^6$ gives **billions** of dollars. Writing the unit in a comment is a good habit. ::: {#63574e3d .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.946600Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.946406Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.959142Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.958140Z"}}' execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} mpd["gdp"] = mpd["gdppc"] * mpd["pop"] / 1e6 # billions of 2011 international dollars mpd["log_gdppc"] = np.log(mpd["gdppc"]) y2018 = mpd[mpd["year"] == 2018] # re-select so it has the new columns y2018.nlargest(5, "gdp")[["country", "gdppc", "pop", "gdp"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ```{=html}
country gdppc pop gdp
3152 China 13101.7064 1.385439e+06 18151.620437
20752 United States 55334.7394 3.278347e+05 18140.645383
9026 India 6806.4986 1.298136e+06 8835.757695
18263 Former USSR 19539.1474 2.944740e+05 5753.769948
10644 Japan 38673.8081 1.258477e+05 4867.010473
``` ::: ::: China's total GDP just exceeds the United States' in 2018 on this measure, while its GDP per capita is about a quarter as large. Level and total are different questions. **Gotcha: `mpd.pop` is not the `pop` column.** `pop` is also the name of a DataFrame *method*, so the dot shortcut `mpd.pop` gives you the method. Always use brackets for column names: `mpd["pop"]`. (`y2018` is a separate copy of the rows; changing it does not change `mpd`.) ::: {#dee15f93 .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.960578Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.960403Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.963525Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.962926Z"}}' execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} type(mpd.pop), type(mpd['pop']) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ``` (method, pandas.Series) ``` ::: ::: **Why logs?** The difference of logs, $\ln y_t - \ln y_{t-1}$, is approximately the growth rate of $y$ (a log difference of $0.02$ is about $2\%$ growth), and equal distances on a log scale are equal percentage changes. Economists use logs for GDP, prices, and populations constantly; Week 5 draws figures with them. ## 5. Missing data Missing values are stored as `NaN` ("not a number"). Count them before deciding what to do: ::: {#ee015605 .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.964960Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.964782Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.975222Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.973933Z"}}' execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(mpd[["gdppc", "pop"]].isna().mean().round(3)) # share missing modern = mpd[mpd["year"] >= 1950].copy() coverage = modern.groupby("year")["gdppc"].count() # count() counts non-missing values print(coverage.loc[[1950, 1970, 1990, 2018]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` gdppc 0.091 pop 0.207 dtype: float64 year 1950 145 1970 153 1990 169 2018 169 Name: gdppc, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: Before 1950 many countries have no estimate, and even since 1950 the number of countries with data changes from year to year (the *sample* changes, which matters when you compare a year-1950 average with a year-2018 average). Most pandas summaries skip missing values by default. Filling them in is a different matter: **don't replace missing with 0**. A missing GDP is not a GDP of zero. ::: {#0232adac .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.976923Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.976742Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.986260Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.985046Z"}}' execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} print("skip missing:", round(mpd["gdppc"].mean(), 1)) print("fillna(0): ", round(mpd["gdppc"].fillna(0).mean(), 1)) print("keep complete rows only:", len(mpd.dropna(subset=["gdppc"])), "of", len(mpd)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` skip missing: 6694.0 fillna(0): 6083.3 keep complete rows only: 19704 of 21682 ``` ::: ::: ## 6. Summaries by group: `groupby` `groupby` splits the table into pieces (one per year, country, region), applies a summary to each, and combines the results. The median is often better than the mean for incomes, because a few very rich countries pull the mean up: ::: {#5c655555 .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.988232Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.988004Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.997335Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.996040Z"}}' execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} by_year = modern.groupby("year")["gdppc"].agg(["count", "median", "mean"]) by_year.loc[[1950, 1980, 2018]].round(0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ```{=html}
count median mean
year
1950 145 2174.0 3927.0
1980 167 6384.0 8616.0
2018 169 12310.0 19012.0
``` ::: ::: To compute growth *within each country*, sort by country and year and take a difference inside each group. `groupby(...).diff()` subtracts the previous row of the **same** country, so the first row of each country is missing: ::: {#d60f48cc .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.999926Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:10.999639Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:11.012507Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:11.011534Z"}}' execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} modern = modern.sort_values(["countrycode", "year"]) modern["growth"] = modern.groupby("countrycode")["log_gdppc"].diff() # log difference, about a growth rate modern["decade"] = (modern["year"] // 10) * 10 (modern.groupby("decade")["growth"].median() * 100).round(2) # median annual growth, percent ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=21} ``` decade 1950 2.25 1960 2.97 1970 2.80 1980 1.06 1990 2.27 2000 3.54 2010 2.24 Name: growth, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: The median country's growth was weakest in the 1980s and strongest in the 2000s. (The 1950s row covers only 1951–59, and the 2010s row only 2011–18. Check what `growth` means where a country has a gap in its years: the difference then spans more than one year. Here the years since 1950 are annual wherever they are present.) ## 7. Combining tables: `merge` `country_groups.csv` is a small table that assigns 26 of the countries to a world region. To attach regions to the GDP data, **merge** the tables on their shared key, `countrycode`: ::: {#ad1008dc .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:11.014343Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:11.014005Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:11.025937Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:11.025069Z"}}' execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} groups = pd.read_csv(f"{DATA}/country_groups.csv") print(groups.head(3)) left = y2018.merge(groups, on="countrycode", how="left") # keep every row of y2018 inner = y2018.merge(groups, on="countrycode", how="inner") # keep only rows found in both print(len(y2018), len(left), len(inner)) print("rows with no region in the left merge:", left["region"].isna().sum()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` countrycode region 0 USA Western Offshoots 1 CAN Western Offshoots 2 AUS Western Offshoots 169 169 26 rows with no region in the left merge: 143 ``` ::: ::: `how="left"` keeps all the country rows and puts `NaN` where there's no match; `how="inner"` keeps only the matches. **After every merge, compare row counts** with what you expected. The most common merge bug is a key that is not unique in one of the tables, which silently multiplies rows. Adding `validate="many_to_one"` makes pandas check, and `indicator=True` records where each row came from. ::: {#601eb5ce .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:11.027564Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:11.027367Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:11.049424Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:11.048023Z"}}' execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} check = mpd.merge(groups, on="countrycode", how="left", validate="many_to_one", indicator=True) print(check["_merge"].value_counts()) dup = pd.concat([groups, groups.iloc[[0]]]) # the USA listed twice by mistake print("extra rows from the duplicate key:", len(mpd.merge(dup, on="countrycode", how="left")) - len(mpd)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` _merge left_only 15032 both 6650 right_only 0 Name: count, dtype: int64 extra rows from the duplicate key: 227 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#52601988 .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:11.052095Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:11.051840Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:11.227529Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:11.226595Z"}}' tags='["raises-exception"]' execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} mpd.merge(dup, on="countrycode", how="left", validate="many_to_one") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

Week 5 builds figures like this one with care. ## 9. Dates and time series `us_macro_1959_2009.csv` has US quarterly data. Dates are the natural index for a time series. Here we build one from the year and quarter columns: ::: {#1aecc5b3 .cell quarto-private-1='{"key":"execution","value":{"iopub.execute_input":"2026-11-21T18:25:11.672057Z","iopub.status.busy":"2026-11-21T18:25:11.671851Z","iopub.status.idle":"2026-11-21T18:25:11.683575Z","shell.execute_reply":"2026-11-21T18:25:11.682409Z"}}' execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code} us = pd.read_csv(f"{DATA}/us_macro_1959_2009.csv") us["date"] = pd.PeriodIndex.from_fields(year=us["year"], quarter=us["quarter"], freq="Q").to_timestamp() us = us.set_index("date") us[["realgdp", "unemp"]].head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=30} ```{=html}
